mcqs.q: Cementum is best described as:
opts: Avascular mineralized connective tissue covering the anatomic root
The soft tissue of the pulp
mcqs.explain: Cementum is the avascular mineralized connective tissue covering the anatomic root, from the CEJ to the apex.

mcqs.q: The main function of cementum is to:
opts: Anchor the periodontal ligament fibres that bind the tooth to the bone
mcqs.explain: Cementum allows attachment of the collagen (Sharpey's) fibres of the periodontal ligament, binding the tooth to the alveolar bone.

mcqs.q: Cementum is thinnest at the ___ and thickest at the ___:
mcqs.explain: Cementum is thinnest at the cementoenamel junction (20–50 µm) and thickest toward the apex (150–200 µm).

mcqs.q: Cementoblasts differentiate mainly from:
opts: Ectomesenchymal cells of the dental follicle (after HERS fragments)
mcqs.explain: As Hertwig's epithelial root sheath fragments, dental-follicle ectomesenchymal cells contact the new root dentin and differentiate into cementoblasts (HERS cells may also transform into cementoblasts).

mcqs.q: Compared with the other mineralized tissues, cementum is:
opts: The least mineralized (~45–50% inorganic) and has the highest fluoride content
mcqs.explain: Cementum is ~45–50% inorganic (least mineralized hard tissue) and has the highest fluoride content of all mineralized tissues.

mcqs.q: The main organic component of cementum is:
mcqs.explain: Type I collagen is the main organic component; non-collagenous proteins include bone sialoprotein, osteopontin and cementum-derived attachment protein (CAP).

mcqs.q: Cementocytes are:
opts: Cementoblasts that became entrapped in lacunae within cellular cementum
mcqs.explain: Cementocytes are cementoblasts incorporated into cellular cementum; they lie in lacunae with canaliculi (processes) directed toward the periodontal surface.

mcqs.q: The processes (canaliculi) of cementocytes are mostly directed toward the:
opts: Periodontal (outer) surface — their source of nutrition
mcqs.explain: Cementocyte canaliculi are directed mainly toward the periodontal surface, from which the cells receive nutrition by diffusion.

mcqs.q: Extrinsic fibres of cementum (Sharpey's fibres) are:
opts: Produced by PDL fibroblasts, larger (5–7 µm), and perpendicular to the surface
Produced by cementoblasts, small, and parallel to the surface
mcqs.explain: Extrinsic (Sharpey's) fibres come from PDL fibroblasts, are larger (5–7 µm) and run perpendicular to the surface; intrinsic fibres are cementoblast-made, small (1–2 µm) and parallel.

mcqs.q: Intrinsic fibres of cementum are produced by:
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic fibres are produced by cementoblasts; they are smaller (1–2 µm) and oriented parallel to the surface.

mcqs.q: The thin unmineralized layer on the cementum surface, lined by cementoblasts, is the:
mcqs.explain: Cementoid is the thin unmineralized surface layer; as a new layer forms, the older one calcifies.

mcqs.q: Incremental lines in cementum represent:
opts: Rest periods, and are more mineralized than adjacent cementum
mcqs.explain: Incremental lines mark rest periods in cementum formation and are more mineralized than the adjacent cementum.

mcqs.q: At the cementoenamel junction (CEJ), the MOST common relationship (~60%) is:
mcqs.explain: In ~60% of teeth cementum overlaps the enamel; ~30% meet in a butt joint; ~10% have a gap (no contact, dentin exposed).

mcqs.q: In ~10% of teeth, the CEJ shows:
opts: A gap where enamel and cementum do not meet (root dentin exposed)
mcqs.explain: In ~10% of teeth, enamel and cementum do not meet, leaving a gap with exposed (sensitive) root dentin.

mcqs.q: The cementodentinal junction (CDJ) is typically:
opts: Smooth in permanent teeth and sometimes scalloped in deciduous teeth
Always deeply scalloped in permanent teeth
mcqs.explain: The CDJ is smooth in permanent teeth and may be scalloped in deciduous teeth; an intermediate cementum layer may seal the root dentin.

mcqs.q: Acellular extrinsic fibre cementum (AEFC) is also called ___ cementum:
opts: Primary (it is formed first; provides anchorage)
mcqs.explain: AEFC is primary cementum (formed first), extends from the cervical margin to the apical third, and its main role is anchorage, especially in single-rooted teeth.

mcqs.q: Cellular cementum is also called ___ cementum:
mcqs.explain: Cellular cementum is secondary cementum (forms later than AEFC); its main functions are adaptation and repair (CIFC + CMSC types).

mcqs.q: Acellular afibrillar cementum (AAC) is characterized by:
opts: No cells AND no extrinsic or intrinsic fibres (a thin coronal layer)
mcqs.explain: AAC contains no cells and no fibres; it is a thin coronal layer (1–15 µm) formed when the reduced enamel epithelium is lost prematurely at the cervical region.

mcqs.q: Which type of cementum contains cementocytes but NO extrinsic fibres?
mcqs.explain: CIFC contains cells (cementocytes) and intrinsic fibres secreted by cementoblasts, but no extrinsic fibres; it fills resorption lacunae in repair.

mcqs.q: Compared with acellular cementum, cellular cementum has:
opts: A faster deposition rate and a more variable width
A slower rate and constant width
mcqs.explain: Cellular cementum is deposited faster, has a highly variable width, contains cementocytes, and its Sharpey's fibres are only partially mineralized.

mcqs.q: Acellular cementum is found chiefly at the ___ of the root:
mcqs.explain: Acellular cementum is found at the cervical third (constant width), whereas cellular cementum predominates at the apical third and interradicular areas.

mcqs.q: The hardness of cementum compared with dentin is:
mcqs.explain: Cementum is softer than dentin; it is light yellow, lacks the luster of enamel and is permeable.

mcqs.q: Cellular mixed stratified cementum (CMSC) is characterized by:
opts: Alternating layers of CIFC and AEFC, mainly in the apical third and furcations
mcqs.explain: CMSC consists of alternating CIFC and AEFC (made by cementoblasts and fibroblasts), occurring mainly in the apical third and furcation areas (100–1000 µm thick).

mcqs.q: Bone sialoprotein in cementum mainly functions to:
mcqs.explain: Among non-collagenous proteins, bone sialoprotein fills the large interfibrillar spaces, osteopontin regulates mineralization, and CAP mediates cell attachment.

saqs.q: Define cementum and give its main function and thickness range.
saqs.a: Avascular mineralized connective tissue covering the anatomic root (CEJ→apex). Function: anchors the PDL fibres. Thinnest at the CEJ (20–50 µm), thickest at the apex (150–200 µm).

saqs.q: How does cementum form (role of HERS)?
saqs.a: Hertwig's epithelial root sheath fragments; dental-follicle ectomesenchymal cells reach the new root dentin and differentiate into cementoblasts (HERS cells may also transform into cementoblasts).
~45–50% inorganic (hydroxyapatite), 50–55% organic + water; type I collagen + non-collagenous proteins (BSP, osteopontin, CAP). Highest fluoride of all mineralized tissues.

saqs.q: Contrast intrinsic and extrinsic fibres of cementum.
saqs.a: Intrinsic: cementoblast-made, small (1–2 µm), parallel to surface. Extrinsic (Sharpey's): PDL fibroblast-made, larger (5–7 µm), perpendicular to surface.
60% cementum overlaps enamel; 30% butt joint (sharp line); 10% gap (enamel and cementum do not meet → exposed dentin).

saqs.q: Compare acellular and cellular cementum (4 points).
saqs.a: Acellular: primary, slower, no cementocytes, constant width, cervical third, well-mineralized Sharpey's. Cellular: secondary, faster, cementocytes in lacunae, variable width, apical third/furcation, partly-mineralized Sharpey's.

saqs.q: Name the detailed types of cementum.
saqs.a: AAC (acellular afibrillar), AEFC (acellular extrinsic fibre = primary), cellular (CIFC + CMSC = secondary), and intermediate cementum.
